chunks: I sat with Ibn 'Abbas when the mention of the ordained shares in inheritances arose. Ibn 'Abbas said: Glory be to Allah, the Most Great! Do you think that He who enumerated the grains of sand in the valley of 'Alij has assigned in an estate a half and a half and a third? These two halves have already consumed the estate — so where is the place for the third?

Zufar ibn Aws al-Basri said to him: O Abu al-'Abbas, who was the first to apply al-'awl to the ordained shares? He replied: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, when the ordained shares crowded together before him and each excluded another. He said: By Allah, I do not know which of you Allah has placed first and which He has placed last, and I find nothing more appropriate than to divide this estate among you in proportional shares — so he imposed upon each person with a right what fell upon him from the reduction of the ordained share. But by Allah, if he had placed first whom Allah placed first, and placed last whom Allah placed last, no ordained share would have exceeded.

Zufar ibn Aws said to him: Which did He place first and which did He place last? He replied: Every ordained share that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought down from its level only to another level — that is what Allah placed first. As for what Allah placed last: every ordained share that, when it moves from its fixed amount, has nothing except what remains — that is what Allah placed last. As for those He placed first: the husband has a half; when something comes to displace him from it, he reverts to a quarter, and nothing displaces him below that. The wife has a quarter; when she is displaced from it, she goes to an eighth, nothing displaces her below that. The mother has a third; when she is displaced from it, she goes to a sixth, nothing displaces her below that — these are the ordained shares Allah, Mighty and Majestic, placed first. As for what Allah placed last: the share of daughters and sisters — they have a half and two-thirds. When the other shares displace them from that, they have nothing but what remains — those are what Allah placed last. When what Allah placed first and what He placed last come together, one begins with what Allah placed first, giving each their complete right. If anything remains, it is for those Allah placed last. If nothing remains, there is nothing for them.

Zufar ibn Aws said to him: What stopped you from advising 'Umar with this view? He replied: His awesomeness. Al-Zuhri said: By Allah, had he presented it to a just Imam whose conduct was based on piety, who would have approved it and put it into effect, no two people would have ever disputed with Ibn 'Abbas concerning knowledge.

key_terms.الْفَرَائِضُ: Ordained shares of inheritance fixed by Quranic law (fara'id)
key_terms.الْمَوَارِيثُ: Inheritances, the laws of estate distribution
key_terms.رَمْلُ عَالِجٍ: The sand of 'Alij (a valley known for vast sand dunes), used as a metaphor for innumerable precision
key_terms.عَوْلُ الْفَرِيضَةِ: Al-'awl: proportional reduction of inheritance shares when they collectively exceed the estate

ai.seo_question: What did Ibn Abbas say about the doctrine of al-'awl (proportional reduction) in Islamic inheritance law?
ai.summary: This hadith records Ibn ‘Abbas’s critique of the doctrine of al-‘awl (proportional reduction of inheritance shares when they exceed the estate), which was introduced by Caliph ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn ‘Abbas argued that God’s ordained shares cannot mathematically exceed 100%, and that ‘Umar’s solution — reducing all shares proportionally — was an error. He presented the correct Shia doctrine: shares of some heirs (husband, wife, mother) are fixed with a fallback tier, and can never be displaced, while others (daughters, sisters) receive only what remains. Al-Zuhri’s closing remark implicitly criticizes the Sunni caliphate: had Ibn ‘Abbas brought this to a just Imam (a Shia reference), the error would have been corrected. The hadith is narrated through an unusual mixed Shia-Sunni chain including al-Zuhri, Ibn Ishaq, and the Zuhri family.
